problem: 'warm its faith' became 'revive its faith' (implies dead faith); 'already' added to the strength of the movement.
replacement: The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present an alarming spectacle. The movement carrying them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so fast that it cannot be guided. Their fate is in their own hands, though in a little while it may no longer be. The first duty of those who direct our affairs at this time is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to replace its inexperience with a knowledge of practical affairs, and its blind impulses with an understanding of its true interests; to adapt its government to time and place; and to change it to suit the events and the people of the age. A new science of politics is needed for a new world. Yet this is what we think about least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we stubbornly fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the abyss.

problem: 'outcasts' rendered 'street children' (changes the image; redundant with 'public streets').
replacement: In no country in Europe has the great social revolution I have been describing advanced as rapidly as in France, but there it has always been carried forward by chance. The heads of the state never planned for its demands, and its victories were won without their consent or without their knowledge. The most powerful, the most intelligent, and the most moral classes of the nation never tried to ally themselves with it in order to guide it. The people were therefore left to their wild impulses, and they grew up like those outcasts who are educated in the public streets and know nothing of society but its vices and its misery. The existence of a democracy seemed to be unknown, until it suddenly took possession of supreme power. Then everything was submitted to its whims, and it was worshipped as the idol of strength. At last, weakened by its own excesses, it was met by lawmakers who rashly conceived the plan of destroying its power instead of instructing it and correcting its vices. No one tried to prepare it to govern. Everyone set about shutting it out of the government.

problem: 'differently gifted by fate' became 'differently treated'; 'religion of art' became 'cult of art'.
replacement: While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the manners of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

problem: 'alike removed from pride and meanness' became 'free of pride and of servility' (meanness = baseness); 'light of intelligence' became 'learning'.
replacement: But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and manners of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.

problem: 'pleasures of enjoyment' rendered 'pleasures of luxury' (changes the contrast with comfort); 'still' added.
replacement: I admit that in a democratic state so constituted, society will not stand still. But the impulses of the social body can be regulated and directed forward. If there is less splendor than in the halls of an aristocracy, the contrast of misery will also be less frequent. The pleasures of enjoyment may be less extreme, but those of comfort will be more widely shared. The sciences may be less perfectly cultivated, but ignorance will be less common. The violence of feeling will be restrained, and the habits of the nation softened. There will be more vices and fewer crimes. Without enthusiasm or ardent faith, great sacrifices may be obtained from the members of a commonwealth by appealing to their understanding and their experience. Each individual will feel the same need to unite with his fellow citizens to protect his own weakness. Knowing that if they are to help him he must cooperate with them, he will readily see that his personal interest is the same as the interest of the community. The nation as a whole will be less brilliant, less glorious, and perhaps less strong. But the majority of citizens will enjoy greater prosperity, and the people will remain quiet, not because they despair of improvement but because they are aware of the advantages of their condition. Not all the consequences of this state of things would be good or useful, but society would at least have taken for itself all those that are. And having renounced the social advantages of aristocracy once and for all, mankind would enter into possession of all the benefits democracy can offer.

problem: 'might hallow by its alliance' became 'could have blessed' (tense/force shift).
replacement: There are zealous Christians among us whose minds are nourished by the love and knowledge of a future life, and who readily take up the cause of human liberty as the source of all moral greatness. Christianity, which has declared all men equal in the sight of God, will not refuse to acknowledge that all citizens are equal in the eyes of the law. But by an odd concurrence of events, religion has become entangled in those institutions that democracy attacks. It is not infrequently driven to reject the equality it loves, and to curse as an enemy the cause of liberty, which it might hallow by its alliance.

In earlier ages, slavery was defended by the venal and the servile-minded, while the independent and the warm-hearted struggled without hope to save the liberties of mankind. But today we meet men of high and generous character whose opinions contradict their inclinations, and who praise a servility they have never known themselves. Others, on the contrary, speak in the name of liberty as if they could feel its sanctity and its majesty, and loudly claim for humanity rights that they have always denied. There are virtuous and peaceable people whose pure morality, quiet habits, affluence, and talents fit them to be the leaders of those around them. Their love of country is sincere, and they are ready to make the greatest sacrifices for its welfare. But they confuse the abuses of civilization with its benefits, and in their minds the idea of evil cannot be separated from that of novelty.
